theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: How does gel nail product harden?
options: It cures under a UV or LED nail lamp
It dries in the air in about an hour
It sets when it is mixed with a powder
It hardens when dipped in cold water

questions.stem: What is the main difference between hard gel and soft (soak-off) gel?
options: Hard gel cures in daylight; soft gel needs a lamp
Hard gel is filed off; soft gel soaks off in acetone
Hard gel is for toes; soft gel is only for the fingers
Hard gel is a polish; soft gel is a powder mix

questions.stem: Why should you use the lamp that the gel maker recommends for that gel?
options: Any lamp will do, as long as it feels warm
Other lamps will change the colour of the gel
The gel needs the right light to cure fully
The maker's lamp is cheaper to run each month

questions.stem: What can happen if gel is under-cured (not fully hardened)?
options: It becomes extra hard and very shiny
It lasts much longer than normal
It turns into a fine powder overnight
It may lift and can cause an allergy

questions.stem: Why should the lamp's bulbs or LEDs be checked and replaced as the maker says?
options: They get brighter with age and may burn the skin
Old bulbs change the colour of the gel polish
New bulbs make the lamp run more quietly
They weaken with age and may not cure the gel

questions.stem: Many gels leave a sticky layer after the final cure. What should be done with it?
options: Leave it on, as it dries by itself overnight
Rinse it off with soap and warm water
Remove it with cleanser on a lint-free wipe
File it off with a coarse 80 grit file

questions.stem: Why is gel put on in thin layers?
options: Thick layers dry in the air more quickly
Thin layers cure fully and give less heat
Thin layers do not need any curing at all
Thick layers would soak into the nail plate

questions.stem: While a nail is curing, the client says it feels very hot. What should you do?
options: Take the hand out briefly, then finish the cure
Hold the hand in so the gel cures more quickly
Blow on the nail but keep it under the lamp
Press the nail down hard until the heat stops

questions.stem: How can the client's skin be protected from the light of a UV nail lamp?
options: Cure each layer twice as long, just to be sure
Let her look into the lamp to check it
Fingerless UV gloves and the right cure time
Use a sunbed tube for a stronger cure

questions.stem: Why should neither you nor the client look straight into the nail lamp?
options: It makes the gel cure unevenly on the nail
The strong light can harm the eyes
It uses up the bulbs much faster
It makes the client feel sleepy

questions.stem: What is the main way that clients and nail technicians become allergic to gel?
options: Uncured gel touching the skin again and again
Looking at the bright light from the nail lamp
Drinking cold water soon after the service
Wearing dark colours of gel polish often

questions.stem: Which signs may show that a client has become allergic to gel?
options: Nails that grow faster than they did before
Shiny nails that stay strong for weeks
A slight smell for a short time after the service
Itching, redness or swelling around the nails

questions.stem: A client shows signs of an allergy to gel. What should you do?
options: Change her to a different brand of gel at once
Stop gel services, record it, and refer her
Cure the gel for longer at her next visit
Put on thicker layers so that it seals in

questions.stem: Why should you not mix gels from different makers in one set?
options: Their colours would always clash
It would make the gel too runny to use
They may not cure or bond well together
The lamp would stop working part-way

questions.stem: Gel has run onto the client's cuticle before it is cured. What should you do?
options: Cure it, then file it off the skin
Leave it, as it will peel off later
Add more gel on top so that it looks neat
Clean it away with a brush before curing

questions.stem: Why should a tiny gap be kept between the gel and the skin?
options: Gel on the skin can cause lifting and allergy
So that the nail can breathe through the gap
So that the gel cures from the sides first
So that the client can see her nail grow

questions.stem: Which is the right way to prepare the natural nail for gel?
options: Push back cuticle, lightly buff, then dehydrate
File hard with a coarse grit until the nail is thin
Soak the nails in warm water for ten minutes
Rub cuticle oil on the nail so that the gel sticks

questions.stem: What does a gel bonder (primer) do?
options: Softens the cuticle so it pushes back
Helps the gel stick to the natural nail
Cures the gel without needing a lamp
Adds extra shine on top of the colour gel

questions.stem: How should the nail desk be made ready between clients?
options: Brush the dust onto the floor and carry on
Spray it with air freshener and then wipe it dry
Clean it, disinfect it and put out a fresh towel
Turn the towel over and use the other side

questions.stem: Which item must be thrown away after one client?
options: A metal cuticle pusher
A glass bowl for soaking
A capped gel brush
A paper file or buffer

questions.stem: Which question is most useful at a gel consultation?
options: How much did you pay for the last set you had?
Which salon did you go to the last time?
Have you reacted to any nail product before?
Do you want the same nails as your friend?

questions.stem: Which condition means you should not apply gel and should refer the client to a doctor?
options: Light ridges along the nail plate
Short nails that are healthy and strong
Pale nails with tiny white spots
Red, swollen skin with pus by the nail

questions.stem: A client takes a medicine that makes her skin sensitive to light. What should you do before using a UV lamp?
options: Cure each layer for double the time
Ask her to check with her doctor first
Use the lamp, but without any gloves
Tell her that it does not matter at all

questions.stem: Before gel goes over a nail tip, what must be done to the tip?
options: Blend away the ridge without filing the nail
Soak it in acetone so that it softens
Leave a ridge on it so that the gel has a grip
Cure it under the lamp for five minutes

questions.stem: Why is the client's finger sometimes turned upside down for a few seconds before builder gel is cured?
options: So that the gel loses its smell
So gravity helps form the apex
So the nail cools before curing
So the gel soaks into the nail

questions.stem: Why should gel be brushed over the very end of the free edge?
options: It seals the edge and helps stop chipping
It makes the nail look longer than it is
It lets the gel cure without the lamp
It hides the nail's natural colour

questions.stem: How long should each gel layer be cured?
options: Until the client says it feels dry
Always five minutes, whatever the gel or lamp
For the time the maker gives for that lamp
For as long as the lamp stays switched on

questions.stem: What is gel polish mainly used for?
options: Building long extensions without tips
Repairing a deep split in the natural nail plate
Filling deep ridges in thick toenails
A thin, glossy colour that lasts for weeks

questions.stem: How should gel pots and bottles be stored?
options: With the lids off, so the gel does not set
On a window ledge, where they are easy to see
In a clear jar right beside the nail lamp
Closed, out of sunlight and away from the lamp

questions.stem: How should gel brushes be looked after?
options: Wash them in hot water at the end of the day
Leave them uncapped beside the nail lamp
Wipe clean and keep capped, out of the light
Soak them in acetone overnight to soften them

questions.stem: Gel cleanser often contains alcohol. What does this mean?
options: It is flammable, so keep it away from heat
It can be used to sterilise all the metal tools
It is safe to drink in small amounts
It cures the gel without using the lamp

questions.stem: Why is extraction needed when filing cured gel?
options: To keep the gel cool while it is being filed
Fine dust can be breathed in and irritate
To make the file cut faster through the gel
To stop the gel from changing its colour

questions.stem: Which is a sign of a well-made gel overlay?
options: Thick at the cuticle so that it lasts longer
Gel on the side walls, to hold it in place
Smooth, even, and thin near the cuticle
A ridge where the tip joins the nail

questions.stem: After the top coat is cured and wiped, what is applied around the nails?
options: Acetone, to clean the skin round them
Cuticle oil, worked into the skin
More bonder, to seal the edges
Gel cleanser, to soften the skin

questions.stem: Which aftercare advice should you give a client with gel nails?
options: Peel the gel off at home when it starts to lift
Use the nails to open cans and scrape labels
Soak the nails in acetone every week to keep them clean
Wear gloves for cleaning and use cuticle oil daily

questions.stem: When should a client usually come back for gel maintenance?
options: In about 2–3 weeks
In about 2–3 days
In about 6 months
Only when the gel falls off

questions.stem: At a gel maintenance visit, what is done with gel that has lifted?
options: File it away gently and blend it before new gel
Glue it down and put fresh gel over it
Pull it off quickly with cuticle nippers
Leave it there, as the new gel will seal it down flat

questions.stem: Why might gel wrinkle or ripple after curing?
options: The lamp was too clean and too bright
The nail was dehydrated before the gel went on
It was put on too thickly, or under-cured
The client's hands were cool and dry

questions.stem: Which is a common cause of gel lifting near the cuticle?
options: Wiping off the sticky layer after the cure
Oil left on the nail, or gel on the skin
Capping the free edge with every layer
Using the lamp the gel maker recommends

questions.stem: What is the safe way to remove soft (soak-off) gel?
options: Peel it off from the side with your nails
Prise it up with a metal pusher and lift
Soak it in hot water until it floats off the nail
Break the top seal, soak, then ease it off

questions.stem: How is hard gel usually removed?
options: It soaks off in acetone in just a few minutes, like polish
It is filed off carefully, as it does not soak off
It peels off once it has been warmed
It is lifted off with cuticle nippers

questions.stem: Why must gel never be peeled or picked off?
options: It makes the gel colour fade on the other nails
It makes the nails grow back much too long
It makes the lamp stop working properly
It pulls off layers of the natural nail too

questions.stem: Where should wipes and cotton with gel or cleanser on them go?
options: Into the open waste basket under the desk
Down the sink, with plenty of running water
Into a lidded bin that is emptied every day
Into the client's bag for her to throw away

questions.stem: A client's skin reacts during a gel service. Where should this be recorded?
options: On her record card, and told to the supervisor
On a sticky note on the lamp for the next client
Nowhere, as long as the reaction goes away
In your phone, to show the client's friends

questions.stem: Why check that the lamp is clean and working before the client arrives?
options: So that the client can buy one from you
So the lamp can warm up for an hour
So that every layer will cure fully
So you can use it to dry normal polish

essays.stem: Explain how to use a UV or LED nail lamp safely and correctly.
essays.modelAnswer: I use the lamp that the gel maker recommends, because each gel needs the right kind of light and time to cure fully. Before the client arrives, I check that the lamp is clean and working and has been looked after as the maker says, because old bulbs or LEDs lose power and can leave the gel under-cured. I check the cord and plug and keep the lamp away from water. I set the timer to the maker's cure time and do not cure for longer than needed. Neither the client nor I look straight into the light. To protect her skin, the client can wear fingerless UV gloves, or put on sunscreen beforehand if she prefers. If she feels a heat spike, she takes her hand out briefly and then puts it back to finish the cure. A client who takes a medicine that makes the skin sensitive to light should check with her doctor first.
markingPoints: Uses the lamp the gel maker recommends, and cures for the maker's time
Checks the lamp, bulbs or LEDs, cord and plug before use, and keeps it away from water
No one looks into the light; fingerless gloves or sunscreen protect the skin
Heat spike: hand out briefly, then finish the cure
A light-sensitive client (from medicine or a condition) checks with her doctor first

essays.stem: Explain how allergies to gel develop, and the steps a nail technician takes to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: Gels contain chemicals called acrylates. When uncured gel touches the skin again and again, the body can become sensitised, which means it starts to react to them. Once a person is allergic, it usually lasts for life, and the reaction can get worse each time. The signs are itching, redness, swelling or blisters around the nails, and sometimes the nail lifts from the bed. To prevent it, I keep a small gap between the gel and the skin and clean away any spill before curing. I apply thin layers and cure each one fully, for the maker's time, in the lamp the maker recommends, because under-cured gel stays soft and can still cause a reaction. I never mix brands in one set. I wear nitrile gloves, do not touch uncured gel, and put used wipes in a lidded bin. If a client shows signs of an allergy, I stop gel services, record it and refer her to a doctor.
markingPoints: Repeated skin contact with uncured gel causes sensitisation, which usually lasts
Signs: itching, redness, swelling or blisters near the nails, or the nail lifting
Gap left from the skin; spills removed before curing
Thin layers fully cured with the right lamp and time; brands never mixed
Technician wears gloves and does not touch uncured gel; a client with signs is stopped, recorded and referred

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a consultation before a gel nail service, including the contraindications you look for.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the client, seat her at a clean desk and explain what will happen. I ask about her health, her medicines (especially any that make the skin sensitive to light), her allergies, any reaction to nail products before, her job and hobbies, and the look and length she wants. I clean both our hands and check her hands and nails in good light. Contraindications include fungal or bacterial infections, swelling, pus, cuts or broken skin, eczema or psoriasis on the hands, a nail lifting from the bed, and signs of an earlier allergy to gel or acrylic. If I find an infection or an allergy, I do not carry out the service. I explain tactfully, without trying to diagnose, and suggest she sees her doctor. If all is well, I agree the service and the price with her, write everything on the record card and ask her to sign it. I keep the card private.
markingPoints: Asks about health, medicines (including light-sensitising ones), allergies and past reactions
Asks about lifestyle and the look wanted, and agrees the service
Cleans hands and checks the hands and nails in good light
Names gel contraindications (infection, broken skin, lifting nail, eczema or psoriasis, earlier allergy)
Does not treat, and refers to a doctor when needed; records on the card with signed consent

essays.stem: Describe the steps for applying soak-off gel polish to natural nails.
essays.modelAnswer: After the consultation, I clean our hands and remove any old polish. I gently push back the cuticle and remove any dead cuticle from the nail plate. I shape the free edge, lightly buff off the shine with a fine buffer and brush away the dust. I wipe the nails with dehydrator and apply a bonder if the maker says so. I apply a thin base coat, keeping it off the skin, cap the free edge and cure it for the maker's time. I apply a thin first coat of colour, cap the edge, clean any spill off the skin with a brush, and cure it. I apply a second thin coat of colour and cure it. Then I apply the top coat, cap the edge and cure it. If a sticky layer is left, I wipe it off with cleanser on a lint-free wipe. I finish with cuticle oil and give the client aftercare advice.
markingPoints: Prepares the nail: cuticle pushed back, shine lightly buffed, dust removed, dehydrated
Thin base coat, capped and cured
Thin coats of colour, each capped and cured; spills cleaned before curing
Top coat capped and cured; sticky layer wiped off with cleanser if there is one
Finishes with cuticle oil and gives aftercare advice

essays.stem: Describe how you would apply builder gel over nail tips, and how you make the nail strong.
essays.modelAnswer: After preparing the nails, I choose a tip for each finger that fits from side wall to side wall, glue it on without air bubbles, cut it to length and blend away the ridge without filing the natural nail. I remove the dust, dehydrate the nails and apply bonder if the maker says so. I brush a thin layer of builder gel over the nail and tip, keeping a small gap from the skin, and cure it. Next I place a bead of builder gel near the middle of the nail and let it settle. I build the apex over the stress area, where the tip meets the natural nail, because this is where the nail bends and breaks. I may turn the finger upside down for a few seconds so that gravity helps to shape the apex, then cure it. I cap the free edge. After curing, I wipe off the sticky layer, file and shape, check the nail from the side and the end, then apply top coat, cure it and finish with oil.
markingPoints: Tips fitted, applied and blended without damaging the natural nail
Preparation: dust removed, dehydrated, bonder as the maker says
A thin first layer, kept off the skin, and cured
Builder gel built into an apex over the stress area (gravity can help) and cured; free edge capped
Sticky layer wiped off, filed, checked from all sides, top coat cured and oil applied

essays.stem: Compare hard gel, soft (soak-off) gel and acrylic for nail enhancements.
essays.modelAnswer: All three make the nail stronger or longer, and all need the same careful preparation. Hard gel is a strong builder gel that cures under the lamp. It can make extensions on tips or forms, and it does not soak off, so it must be filed off with care. It has little smell. Soft gel, which includes gel polish and some builder gels, also cures under the lamp, but it can be soaked off in acetone. It is thinner and more flexible, so it suits natural nails and short overlays rather than long extensions. Acrylic is a liquid monomer mixed with a powder. It sets by a chemical reaction at room temperature, with no lamp, has a strong smell and needs good extraction. It is very strong and is soaked off in acetone. All three can cause an allergy if the product touches the skin. The choice depends on the client's nails, lifestyle, the length she wants, any allergies, and the technician's training.
markingPoints: Hard gel: cures in the lamp, is strong, and must be filed off
Soft gel: cures in the lamp, soaks off in acetone, thinner, for natural nails and overlays
Acrylic: liquid and powder, sets with no lamp, strong smell needing extraction, soaks off
All need good preparation and can cause allergy if they touch the skin
The choice depends on the client's nails, lifestyle, length and allergies

essays.stem: Describe how to remove soft (soak-off) gel safely, and explain why it must never be peeled off.
essays.modelAnswer: I make sure the area is well ventilated, wear gloves and keep the acetone away from heat and flames. I gently file the shiny top coat to break the seal, so that the acetone can get in, taking care not to reach the natural nail. I put cuticle oil or barrier cream on the skin around the nails. I place a cotton pad soaked in acetone on each nail and wrap it in foil, or use remover clips, and leave it for the time the maker says. I check one nail first. When the gel has softened, I gently ease it off with a wooden stick, working from the cuticle towards the free edge. If some is still stuck, I wrap it again rather than force it. Then I buff lightly, wash the hands and apply cuticle oil. Peeling gel off pulls away layers of the natural nail with it, leaving the nail thin, weak and sore, and more likely to split or become infected.
markingPoints: Ventilation, gloves, and acetone kept from heat and flames
Top seal filed to break it, without filing the natural nail
Skin protected; acetone-soaked cotton and foil left for the maker's time
Softened gel eased off gently with a wooden stick; rewrapped rather than forced
Explains that peeling removes layers of the nail, leaving it thin, weak and sore

essays.stem: Describe three common problems with gel nails, their causes, and how to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: Lifting is when the gel comes away from the nail, often near the cuticle. It is caused by oil, dust or dead cuticle left on the nail, by gel touching the skin, or by under-curing. I prevent it with careful preparation, a small gap from the skin and full cures. Wrinkling or rippling happens when gel is put on too thickly, so the top cures but the gel underneath stays soft, or when the lamp is weak. I prevent it with thin layers and a lamp that is checked and matched to the gel. A heat spike is a sudden burning feeling while curing, because the gel gives off heat as it hardens. Thick layers and very thin, over-filed nails make it worse. I use thin layers and avoid over-filing; if it happens, the client takes her hand out briefly, then finishes the cure. Chipping at the tip is prevented by capping the free edge with each layer.
markingPoints: Lifting: poor preparation, gel on the skin or under-curing; prevented by good preparation, a gap and full cures
Wrinkling: thick layers or a weak lamp; prevented with thin layers and the right lamp
Heat spike: heat given off while curing, worse with thick gel or thin nails; hand out briefly
Another problem, such as chipping prevented by capping, or allergy prevented by keeping gel off the skin
Causes and prevention are matched correctly

essays.stem: Explain how you keep yourself and the client safe from the chemicals and the dust used in gel services.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the safety data sheet for each product and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules. I keep the room well ventilated and use desk extraction when filing, because cured gel dust is fine and can be breathed in. I wear a dust mask and safety glasses when filing, and nitrile gloves when handling gel and cleanser. I never let uncured gel touch my skin or the client's. Gel cleanser and acetone are flammable, so I keep them away from heat and flames and close the lids after use. Gels are stored closed in their labelled containers, out of sunlight and away from the lamp, so that they do not start to cure. Wipes and cotton with product on them go in a lidded bin that is emptied each day. I do not eat or drink at the desk. If a product gets in an eye, I rinse it with plenty of clean running water and get medical help.
markingPoints: Reads the safety data sheet; follows the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Ventilation and extraction; dust mask and safety glasses when filing
Nitrile gloves; no uncured gel on anyone's skin
Cleanser and acetone kept from heat and flames; gels stored closed and out of the light
Lidded bin for waste; no food or drink; an eye splash rinsed with plenty of water and medical help sought

essays.stem: Describe the aftercare and maintenance advice you would give a client after a gel service, and say why each point matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I tell the client to wear gloves for washing up, cleaning and gardening, because water and chemicals weaken the gel and dry the skin. She should not use her nails as tools, because this can chip or lift them. She should rub cuticle oil into the skin around the nails every day, to keep the skin and nails supple. She must not peel or pick the gel if it lifts, because that takes layers of the natural nail with it and lets water and germs in; she should come back for a repair instead. She should return for maintenance or a professional removal in about 2–3 weeks, so that the new growth can be infilled or the gel taken off safely. If she has itching, redness or swelling around the nails, she should come back at once or see a doctor, because it may be an allergy. I write the advice I gave on her record card.
markingPoints: Gloves for wet work and cleaning
Do not use the nails as tools
Cuticle oil every day
Never peel or pick; return for repair, maintenance or removal in about 2–3 weeks
Report itching, redness or swelling; advice written on the record card

practical1.title: Nail tips with a builder gel overlay on a partner's nails
practical1.brief: As a group, set up safe nail stations in the Centre's salon, with good ventilation, desk extraction and a lamp that matches the gel system. Use one maker's gel system only. Work in a circle: each member is the nail technician for the next member, who agrees to be the client, so that everyone is both technician and client. Each technician checks the lamp, carries out a consultation, checks for contraindications and fills in a record card that the client signs. The technician then prepares two nails, fits and blends tips, and applies a builder gel overlay with an apex over the stress area, curing each thin layer for the maker's time. Shape, finish and give aftercare advice. If a member has a contraindication, or does not agree to be a client, the technician works on a practice hand instead. Each member also takes one job for the group: setting up, checking the lamps and extraction, taking the photos, or leading the clean-down. Photograph each stage below, showing only hands and nails, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group, with the record cards.
materials: Nail desks with good lighting and desk extraction
A UV or LED lamp that matches the gel system, checked before use
One maker's gel system: bonder, builder gel, top coat and gel cleanser, in labelled containers
Gel brushes with caps
Nail tips in a range of sizes, nail adhesive and tip cutters
Files (100/180 and 180/240 grit), buffers and dust brushes
Cuticle pushers, orange sticks, dehydrator, lint-free wipes and cuticle oil
Fingerless UV gloves for clients
Nitrile gloves, dust masks and safety glasses
Record cards and pens
A bin with a lid, disinfectant, paper towels and fresh towels
A practice hand for any member who cannot be a client
Phone or tablet for photos
photos: The stations set up, with the lamp, one gel system and the lidded bin
Each member's completed record card, with the client's name covered
The two nails prepared, with the tips fitted and blended
Builder gel applied before curing, showing the gap at the cuticle
The hand in the lamp, with the client wearing a fingerless glove
The two finished nails: top view and side view
The stations cleaned, tools disinfected and waste in the lidded bin
checklist: Carried out a consultation, checked for contraindications and got signed consent
Checked the lamp and used one maker's gel system with its matching lamp
Prepared the natural nails correctly, without over-filing
Fitted and blended the tips with no ridge
Applied thin layers, kept gel off the skin, cleaned spills before curing and capped the free edge
Cured each layer for the maker's time and dealt correctly with any heat spike
Built a balanced apex over the stress area, with a smooth, even finish
Wiped off any sticky layer, finished with oil, gave aftercare advice and cleaned the station
safety: Use only the lamp that matches the gel, for the maker's cure time; do not look into the light
Keep uncured gel off everyone's skin, and wear nitrile gloves
Do not mix brands in one set; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep cleanser and acetone away from heat and flames, and close the lids
Use the extraction, and wear a dust mask and safety glasses when filing
Do not work on anyone with an infection, broken skin or a known allergy to nail products

practical2.title: Gel polish on natural nails, and safe soak-off removal
practical2.brief: As a group, set up safe nail stations with good ventilation and a lamp that matches the gel polish system. Work in a circle again: each member is the technician for the next member, who agrees to be the client. Part 1: after a consultation and contraindication check, each technician prepares the natural nails of one hand and applies soak-off gel polish (base coat, two thin coats of colour and top coat), capping and curing each layer for the maker's time and keeping gel off the skin. The assessor checks the finished nails. Part 2: each technician then safely removes soak-off gel from two of the client's nails (gel from an earlier service, or two of the nails just done once they have been photographed and checked), using the break-the-seal, wrap and ease-off method, and finishes with oil and aftercare advice. Each member also takes one job for the group: setting up, checking the lamps, taking the photos, or leading the clean-down. Photograph each stage below, showing only hands and nails, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group, with the record cards.
materials: Nail desks with good lighting and desk extraction
A UV or LED lamp that matches the gel polish system, checked before use
One maker's soak-off gel polish system: bonder, base coat, colours, top coat and gel cleanser
Fine files, buffers, dust brushes, cuticle pushers and orange sticks
Dehydrator, lint-free wipes and cuticle oil
Acetone, cotton pads and foil wraps or remover clips
Barrier cream or cuticle oil to protect the skin during removal
Fingerless UV gloves for clients
Nitrile gloves, dust masks and safety glasses
Record cards and pens
A bin with a lid, disinfectant, paper towels and fresh towels
Phone or tablet for photos
photos: The stations set up, with the lamp, one gel system and the lidded bin
The nails prepared: cuticles pushed back, shine buffed off and dehydrated

Removal: the top seal broken and the nails wrapped in cotton and foil
